steps.body: Sometimes the place you'd normally break from is itself a **zero** — and zero has nothing to lend. When that happens, reach one place FURTHER left. If that's zero too, keep reaching until you find a digit that isn't zero, break IT, and every zero you passed through becomes a 9 along the way.
Watch the chain reach past two zeros.

widget.prompt: Walk through 40,052 − 18,675 one column at a time.

panels.title: Ones
panels.body: 2 is smaller than 5. The tens digit (5) isn't zero, so break it directly: tens becomes 4, ones becomes 12. 12 − 5 = 7.

panels.title: Tens — the zero problem
panels.body: Tens is now 4, smaller than 7. Look left: hundreds is 0 — nothing to lend. Look further: thousands is ALSO 0. Keep reaching: ten-thousands is 4 — not zero. Break IT.

panels.title: The chain resolves
panels.body: Ten-thousands (4) breaks to 3. Every zero it passed through — thousands AND hundreds — becomes 9. Tens becomes 14. 14 − 7 = 7.

panels.title: Finish the columns
panels.body: Hundreds is now 9: 9 − 6 = 3. Thousands is now 9: 9 − 8 = 1. Ten-thousands is now 3: 3 − 1 = 2. The answer is 21,377.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep tracing the chain past each zero.
widget.successFeedback: 40,052 − 18,675 = 21,377 — the break reached past two zeros, turning both into 9s along the way.

predict.prompt: Borrowing when the very next column holds a ZERO — does the borrow just stop there?

options.label: No — it chains left until a nonzero digit

predict.reveal: A zero has nothing to lend, so it borrows too — the request relays leftward until someone can pay, and the zeros become nines along the way.

explanationVariants: 5,003 has two zeros between the 5 and the 3. The break reaches all the way to the thousands digit (5→4), turning both zeros into 9s, giving 3,156.
The thousands digit lends 1, and both zeros it passes become 9.

commonErrors.feedback: 4,844 subtracted the smaller digit from the larger in each column, ignoring which number is on top. Reaching the break past both zeros gives 3,156.
4,156 didn't break the thousands digit far enough — it needs to reach past BOTH zeros. Doing that gives 3,156.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Find the nearest nonzero digit to the left, break it, and turn every zero in between into a 9.

steps.body: The chain can reach as far left as it needs to. It doesn't matter if there's one zero in the way or several — the rule is identical: find the first nonzero digit, break it, and every zero between it and the column that needs help becomes a 9.

explanationVariants: 500,203 has one small chain near the ones and another chain near the front — working through both carefully gives 412,747.
Each borrow episode is handled the same way, one at a time, right to left.

commonErrors.feedback: 587,253 subtracted the smaller digit from the larger in each column, ignoring which number is on top. Breaking correctly through both zero-chains gives 412,747.
413,747 is one break short in an early column. Re-checking each zero-chain carefully gives 412,747.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Work column by column from the ones; wherever a break is needed, reach past any zeros to the first nonzero digit.

steps.body: How far does the chain reach?

explanationVariants: Every zero digit the chain reaches through becomes a 9 — it received 10, then lent 1 onward, leaving 9.
The zeros aren't skipped; each one flips to 9 as the chain passes.

widget.prompt: When a borrow chain reaches past two zero digits to find a nonzero one, what happens to those two zeros?

options.label: Both become 9
options.feedback: Each zero receives 10 (becoming 10), then immediately lends 1 onward to the next column, leaving 9.

options.label: They stay 0
options.feedback: They can't stay 0 — each one both receives and lends a borrow, which lands them at 9, not 0.

options.label: They become 10
options.feedback: 10 isn't a valid single digit. Each zero receives 10 then immediately lends 1 forward, settling at 9.

options.label: Only the nearer one changes
options.feedback: Every zero the chain passes through changes — each one becomes 9, not just the nearest.

hints: 600,004 has FOUR zeros in a row between its first digit and its last.

Every zero it passes — ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds, and tens — becomes a 9.
explanationVariants: 600,004's borrow chain reaches past four zeros to the hundred-thousands digit (6→5), turning all four into 9s. The result is 364,526.
Four zeros flip to 9 in one single chain, the longest reach in this course.

steps.body: The chain, however long it needs to be.
takeaways: If the digit you'd break is zero, reach one place further — and keep reaching until you find a nonzero digit.
Every zero the chain passes through becomes a 9, not a 0 and not a 10.
The chain can be as long as it needs to be — one zero, two zeros, or four.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **When the digit next door is zero, reach past it to the next nonzero digit — and that zero becomes a 9.** For 703 − 256: ones (3) needs a break, but tens is 0. Reach to hundreds (7→6); tens becomes 9. Ones becomes 13. 13−6=7, 9−5=4, 6−2=4. Result: 447.

explanationVariants: The break reaches past the zero tens digit to the hundreds (7→6); tens becomes 9. Result: 447.
One zero flips to 9 in this chain.

options.feedback: Reach past the zero tens digit to hundreds (7→6), tens becomes 9: 13−6=7, 9−5=4, 6−2=4.
553 subtracted the smaller digit from the larger in each column. Reaching the break past the zero gives 447.
543 didn't flip the zero tens digit to 9. Doing that correctly gives 447.
